slope.demName: LOLA LDEM_60S_60M, 60 m site window, 60 m

provenance.ephemerisNote: In-app model (astronomy-engine + IAU lunar rotation, light-time and aberration applied, airless): within 0.004 deg of JPL Horizons topocentric airless az/el (DE441) in all validation samples 1969-2035. Directions computed every 3 h and interpolated (agreeing with the model to better than 0.0005 deg).
terrainNotes: Elevation data at this point, finest first: LOLA LDEM_60S_60M, 60 m site window (60 m per sample, to about 3.8 km); LOLA LDEM_60S_60M, 480 m site window (480 m per sample, to about 31 km); LOLA whole-Moon grid, 16 px/deg (1.9 km per sample, whole Moon).
Beyond about 31 km from the site only the whole-Moon grid is available (1.9 km per sample), which smooths ridges narrower than that; distant skyline peaks can read slightly low.

Where one grid hands over to the next, the heights do not match exactly; the grids are used as stored, so the ground steps there: 3.8 km from the site the 60 m window ends and the 480 m window takes over, lying between 21.3 m below and 22.7 m above it, 6.6 m RMS (1 m of height is 0.015° of skyline there); 31 km from the site the 480 m window ends and the whole-Moon grid takes over, lying between 221 m below and 126 m above it, 52.5 m RMS (1 m of height is 0.002° of skyline there). A skyline point formed right at such an edge is uncertain by about that much.
assumptions: Observer 2 m above the terrain at -69.3741, 32.3200 (degrees, east-positive, ME frame); heights above the 1737.4 km sphere.
Positions are topocentric and airless (no refraction), as JPL Horizons APPARENT=AIRLESS for a coord@301 observer.

Skyline from elevation data, including the Moon's curvature, 0.5 deg in azimuth, searched to 173 km: LOLA LDEM_60S_60M, 60 m site window (60 m) from 0.0 to 5.4 km; LOLA LDEM_60S_60M, 480 m site window (480 m) from 3.9 to 43.2 km; LOLA whole-Moon grid, 16 px/deg (1895 m) from 30.8 to 173.1 km.
Sampled every 5 min; rise and set times refined to 10 s; the Sun and Earth are discs (visible fraction integrated across each disc).

A rise or set takes time, so each event is one named instant (decision D-8): sunrise = the first part of the Sun's disc appears above the skyline ("Sun starts rising"), sunset = the last part goes behind it ("Sun fully set"); Earthrise / Earthset = Earth's centre crossing the skyline. Each event's span (and `transitions`) gives the whole passage: from the first cut of the disc to the last limb when setting, from the first limb to the whole disc clear when rising.
Sunlight also counts Earth passing in front of the Sun (geometric discs; the faint light refracted by Earth's atmosphere is ignored).

Earth visibility is geometric line of sight only; it says nothing about a working radio link. "Earth in view" (earthVisiblePct) counts Earth's centre above the skyline; earthAnyPct counts any part of Earth's disc, the definition of the PGDA long-term Earth map.
Slope over a 120 m baseline from LOLA LDEM_60S_60M, 60 m site window, 60 m: hazards smaller than the grid are not seen.

warnings: Beyond about 31 km from the site only the whole-Moon grid is available (1.9 km per sample), which smooths ridges narrower than that; distant skyline peaks can read slightly low.

station.name: Madrid DSS-63 (70 m)
station.complex: Robledo de Chavela, near Madrid, Spain

assumptions: Geometry only: an opportunity is an unobstructed straight line between the station and the site, with the site above the station's elevation limit and the station above the site's terrain skyline. It is not a statement about a working radio link: no link budget, frequency, antenna pattern, antenna scheduling or availability is considered.

Stations: the 70 m antennas DSS-14 (Goldstone), DSS-43 (Canberra) and DSS-63 (Madrid). Coordinates from the DSN Telecommunications Link Design Handbook, 810-005, Module 301 Rev. N (15 April 2022), Tables 2 and 5 (ITRF93 epoch 2003.0; WGS 84).

Elevation limits: 6.0 deg for receiving (the handbook's generic receive limit; the antennas' mechanical limit is about 6 deg) and, for transmitting, 10.4 deg at DSS-14 and 10.2 deg at DSS-43 and DSS-63 (the limits of the handbook's 70 m transmit coverage chart). The stations' own azimuth-dependent horizon masks are not applied: for instance the handbook keeps DSS-63 above 20.2 deg towards high ground to its north-west when transmitting, and high-power transmitters have higher limits.
At the site the direction to the station itself is tested against the skyline (the stations are up to 0.95 deg from the centre of Earth's disc).

Positions are geometric and airless (no tropospheric refraction); Earth's rotation uses UT1 = UTC (the two differ by at most 0.9 s) without polar motion. Checked against JPL Horizons, the site as seen from each station: elevation within 0.0013 deg over 1154 instants (1971, 2025, 2034), and within 0.0010 deg in an independent check on three other dates. The edges of each opportunity, where a station reaches its elevation limit or goes behind the lunar skyline, are placed by bisection to 0.25 s; an edge set by the skyline rests on the elevation data there.
